problem_framing.rationale: Answers the question exactly as posed ('should we, and if so how') with a segment-specific yes in the first line. Uses the stated objectives as criteria: the 15% ARR target is bridged on slide 13 ($98.9M target, $0.6M gap), the NRR floor is checked (114% vs 100%), and the renewal-only and enterprise-contract constraints drive the correction of the $10.3M. Identifies early what the answer turns on: cohort versus rate effect in SMB, where pricing power sits, and what a rise is really worth. Addresses the CFO, CEO and Customer Success views directly. Nothing material missing.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the four summary points are the four sections, and nearly every title is a claim backed by its slide; titles alone give the argument. Flaws: the headline diagnosis ('not because customers reject today's prices') sits uneasily with slide 6's own finding that the cohort 'quit when full price arrived' and 'is the one group that reacts to price'; the nuance is in the body but not in the summary line the CEO reads first. Slide 6's title overstates its evidence (most cohort customers have not quit), and slide 14's title compares an enterprise break-even with an SMB precedent. The modest mid-market churn rise (0.6% to 0.8%) is noted but left unexplained while the summary attributes rising churn to the promotion alone.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-did every calculation and found no numerical errors. Promotion-cohort churn 4.9% ((182.9 − 79.8) / 2,100); reachable uplift $7.566M with a correct waterfall (−0.738, −1.728, −0.288); blended churn 1.7%→2.6% and ARR-weighted 0.8%→1.2%; break-evens p/(1+p) of 6.5%, 7.4%, 9.1%; 2023 extra loss 3.6%; NRR bridge $94.0M; segmented uplift $4.27M; 32% churn cut; $1.3M SMB test value. All critical evidence is used, including evidence against the answer (Inkwell, the new-sign-up limitation of the 2024 test, the pre-Inkwell 2023 precedent), and assumptions are footnoted. Not a 5 because several claims overreach: 'most promotion customers… quit' (the pack says most of those who left did so within two months; 2,100 remain in the base), 'far beyond any past response' (one SMB precedent, none for mid-market or enterprise renewals), and the 0.1 pp residual called 'the lasting cost of the 8% rise'. The 'only $0.6M to find' bridge rests on trailing NRR repeating with zero churn response; this is footnoted but headlined with more confidence than it warrants.

strategic_judgment.rationale: A clear, segment-differentiated recommendation that follows from the analysis and matches a defensible route: raise mid-market and enterprise within caps, hold SMB behind a controlled test, treat activation as a separate lever. The CFO's plan is compared in dollars and risk ($3.3M more on paper, three-quarters from SMB); the Customer Success claim is tested and discounted (a third, not a half; no evidence for effect size). Says what would change the answer: SMB go/no-go on the test read-out, a stop rule tied to quantified break-evens, and a monthly mid-market read. Next steps have owners and dates. Avoids all five traps. Minor reservations, not enough to drop a point: the stop threshold ('approach break-even') is loose, no structural SMB response to Inkwell (lower tier, grandfathering) is considered, and the activation programme has no cost.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: Answer is in the first line of the executive summary with page references; language is plain and precise, and derivations are shown compactly. Twenty slides including four section dividers, an appendix divider and a backup is somewhat more than the decision needs, and the summary repeats on each divider. Slide 14's mixed comparison and the '7–10%' enterprise shorthand take a moment to decode.

unsupported_claims.quote: Most promotion customers never set up the product and quit when full price arrived
unsupported_claims.why: The pack says most promotion customers who left did so within two months of the discount ending, not that most of the cohort left; 2,100 are still in the base. The 41% figure is a first-month activity measure, not 'never set up'.

unsupported_claims.quote: Churn would have to jump far beyond any past response
unsupported_claims.why: There is one past response, an 8% SMB rise before Inkwell. There is no renewal precedent for mid-market or enterprise at 10%, so 'any past response' overstates the basis.

unsupported_claims.quote: After it settled: churn stayed just above the old level, the lasting cost of the 8% rise
unsupported_claims.why: Attributes the 0.1 pp residual (1.8% to 1.9%) causally to the price rise; the pack gives no basis for separating it from noise or other factors.

unsupported_claims.quote: Churn is rising because of the 2025 SMB promotion, not because customers reject today's prices
unsupported_claims.why: Overstated as a headline: 52% of cohort churners cite price and left when full price arrived, and mid-market churn also rose (0.6% to 0.8%) for reasons the promotion cannot explain. The body is more balanced than this line.

unsupported_claims.quote: Board dashboard (measure not defined): 1.4% H1 2025, 2.3% H1 2026
unsupported_claims.why: The pack gives the dashboard figures as '1.4% → 2.3%' in a Q2 2026 dashboard without stating the periods; the H1 labels are assumed.

recommendation.summary: Raise prices by segment in 2027: +10% at mid-market renewals and +7% (capped) to +10% at enterprise renewals from January, worth about $4.3M. Hold SMB prices, run an 8% controlled renewal test on non-promotion SMB in Q1 with a go/no-go in April, run an activation programme for the promotion cohort with price held, and define one churn measure by segment for the board.
recommendation.rationale: Meets all four defensibility criteria. It separates the mix effect from the rate effect (cohort 4.9% vs non-promotion 2.1%, flat against 2.0%). It reconciles the CFO and CEO views ('both views hold for this cohort'). It corrects the $10.3M to about $7.6M using renewal timing and the 7% cap. It differentiates pricing by segment, with a staged SMB test and break-even stop rules.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The CFO's hypothesis is revised rather than adopted or rejected. The document agrees that the churn rise is mostly the promotion cohort (mix effect about 1.0 pp of 1.1 pp), but shows that this cohort is also the price-sensitive group and that Inkwell makes SMB risky, so the CEO's concern holds for SMB. It corrects the $10.3M to $7.6M, replaces the flat 12% with a segmented plan, and discounts the 'halve SMB churn' claim to about a third at best. It flags the new-sign-up limitation of the 2024 test, the pre-Inkwell date of the 2023 precedent and the undefined dashboard metric. The two causal overreaches are the 0.1 pp residual called 'the lasting cost of the 8% rise' and the headline 'not because customers reject today's prices', which is more one-sided than the body.

output.overall_comment: Very strong document. Every required calculation is done and checks out against the pack: cohort churn 4.9%, $7.57M reachable uplift, blended and ARR-weighted churn, break-even thresholds and the 2023 extra loss of 3.6%. It uses all critical evidence, avoids all five traps, and lands on a segment-differentiated recommendation with a staged SMB test, stop rules, owners and dates. Weaknesses are mostly wording that outruns the evidence: 'most promotion customers… quit', 'far beyond any past response', and a headline diagnosis more one-sided than the body's own 'both views hold'. The 'only $0.6M to find' growth bridge leans on trailing NRR repeating with no churn response; this is footnoted but fragile. No structural SMB response to Inkwell is considered, the stop threshold is loosely specified, and the deck is somewhat longer than the decision needs. Weighted score is 4.40.
